question: What makes an injection truly safe in clinical practice?

options.A: It must always be given intravenously
options.B: It utilizes multi-dose vials for cost efficiency
options.C: It harms no one and creates zero dangerous waste
options.D: It is administered only by senior medical doctors

explanation: A safe injection keeps everyone protected—the patient, you as the nurse, and the community—from injury and hazardous waste. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h1)

question: Why do many patients in local communities often prefer injections over tablets?

options.A: Injections are proven to have zero side effects
options.B: National health insurance only covers parenteral drugs
options.C: Oral medications are completely unavailable in local pharmacies
options.D: They believe injections work much faster in the body

explanation: Many patients feel that because an injection goes straight into the body, it must cure them quicker than swallowing a pill. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h1)

question: Which infection-causing agent attacks CD4+ T-cells and can spread through dirty needles?
explanation: HIV specifically targets and weakens the body's immune defenses by destroying CD4+ T-lymphocytes. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h2)

question: How do germs usually enter a patient's body during an unsafe injection?

options.A: Through intact skin without any mechanical breach
options.B: By mutating inside the human bloodstream after exposure
options.C: Through contaminated multi-dose vials or unsterile equipment
options.D: Via airborne droplets released during medication reconstitution

explanation: Bacteria and other germs get in when equipment isn't sterile or when proper clean technique is missed during preparation. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h2)

question: What are the classic warning signs of an acute viral hepatitis infection?

options.C: Sudden paralysis of the lower limbs

explanation: When the liver is inflamed, it struggles to process bilirubin, leading to yellow eyes and skin (jaundice) and dark urine. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h3)

question: A patient has a swollen, hot, and pus-filled injection site. What is the most likely cause?
explanation: Heat, swelling, and pus right at the puncture site are classic clues that bacteria managed to enter during the procedure. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h3)

question: Why do shortages of disposable syringes lead to dangerous injection practices?

options.A: They force nurses to administer all drugs orally
options.B: They tempt personnel to reuse single-use equipment
options.C: They prevent patients from visiting hospitals entirely
options.D: They cause medications to expire faster on shelves

explanation: When basic supplies run out, stressed healthcare workers might feel pressured to reuse items meant only for one person. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a major system challenge causing unsafe injections in Nigeria?

options.C: Operations of unregistered patent medicine vendors
options.D: Irregular power supply in rural health facilities

explanation: Having plenty of safe supplies actually stops unsafe practices! Shortages and unlicensed sellers are the real problems. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h4)

question: What is the single most important action a nurse can take to stop the spread of infection?
explanation: Good old-fashioned handwashing removes germs before they can be passed on to the next patient. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h5)

question: When should you take off non-sterile gloves during patient care?

options.A: Immediately after completing the task for that patient
options.B: Only at the end of an eight-hour nursing shift
options.C: Whenever hands begin to feel warm

explanation: Always remove your gloves right after finishing with a patient so you don't carry their germs to the next task. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why is putting the cap back on used needles (recapping) strongly discouraged?

options.A: It violates international medication storage laws
options.B: It dulls the sharp tip making subsequent injections painful
options.C: It chemically alters the medication left inside the barrel
options.D: It is the leading cause of accidental needle-stick injuries

explanation: Trying to guide a tiny needle back into its plastic cap is how most nurses accidentally prick their own fingers. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h6)

question: When should a sharps container be safely closed and replaced?
explanation: Sealing the box at the three-quarters mark stops needles from spilling over or poking through when people try to squeeze more in. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is the very first thing you should do if you accidentally get poked by a used needle?

options.A: Cover the puncture wound with strong adhesive tape
options.B: Wash the site gently with soap and running water
options.C: Apply a tourniquet tightly above the injured site
options.D: Squeeze the wound aggressively to drain all blood

explanation: Wash the area gently with soap and clean water. Avoid squeezing or scrubbing hard, as that can push germs deeper. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h7)

question: Why is acting quickly so important after an accidental needle-stick exposure to HIV?

options.A: Late initiation makes the drugs permanently inactive
options.B: Prophylaxis must begin within hours to be most effective
options.C: Delayed treatment causes permanent liver failure
options.D: Baseline blood tests expire after twelve hours

explanation: Post-exposure drugs work best when started right away, before the virus has a chance to take hold in the body. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h7)

question: How can community health nurses help stop unsafe injection habits?

options.A: By distributing free multi-dose vials to local families
options.B: By encouraging patients to reuse syringes at home
options.C: By replacing all doctors in rural health posts
options.D: By educating the public against unnecessary parenteral drug use

explanation: Teaching communities helps people understand when pills work just as well, reducing the demand for needless injections. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h8)

question: A patient is worried that oral antibiotics won't work as fast as an injection. How do you respond?

options.A: Tell the patient to seek care at a traditional healer instead
options.B: Quietly administer an unprescribed injection to satisfy the patient
options.C: Insist that injections are always dangerous and should never be used
options.D: Explain how oral medications work effectively while remaining much safer

explanation: Listen to their worries with respect, then gently explain how safe, effective oral medications are a great choice. [learn more](GNS122_U3_T3#GNS122_U3_T3_h8)
